results.title: Chapter 8: Beam Bending, Buckling, and Torsion - Engineering LibreTexts
results.snippet: Open-access university textbook chapter that derives and confirms the core cheat-sheet formulas the skill must verify: bending stress sigma = Mc/I (flexure formula), torsion tau = Tr/J, Euler-Bernoulli deflection (EI flexural rigidity, d2v/dx2 = M/EI), and Euler buckling P_cr = pi^2 EI / l^2. Useful as a single citable source to confirm the materials-mechanics formulas are stated correctly, including the variable definitions (c = distance to outer fiber, I = second moment of area, J = polar moment, r = radius).

results.title: Factor of safety - Wikipedia
results.snippet: Confirms the two distinct definitions the skill must keep straight: design factor vs realized factor of safety, and that FoS is referenced to yield strength for ductile materials and ultimate strength for brittle materials. Good for checking the 'safety factor / margin' verification gate and flagging the common red-flag error of mixing yield- and ultimate-based definitions or conflating margin of safety (MS = FoS - 1) with FoS.

results.title: Buckling - Wikipedia
results.snippet: Confirms Euler critical load P_cr = pi^2 EI / (KL)^2 and, crucially, the effective-length factor K for boundary conditions (pinned-pinned K=1, fixed-free K=2, fixed-fixed K=0.5) plus the slenderness-ratio validity limit beyond which Euler's formula applies (else Johnson/inelastic buckling). Directly addresses a classic red flag: applying the Euler formula outside its slenderness range, or omitting the end-condition factor.

results.title: Bolt Torque Calculator — Preload and Clamp Force | FIRGELLI
results.snippet: Confirms the bolt cheat-sheet formula T = K*D*F with T = torque, K = nut/torque factor, D = nominal bolt diameter, F = preload, and the default K = 0.2 for unknown/as-received steel conditions. Lets the skill verify the bolt-torque equation and flag the standard caveat that torque-based preload is inherently scattered (±25-35%) due to friction variability.

results.title: Nut Factor K Values - Dissecting the Nut Factor | Peak Innovations
results.snippet: Industry engineering article dissecting the nut factor K in T=KDF, giving the range of K values by lubrication/plating condition (roughly 0.10 lubricated to 0.30 dry/plated, 0.20 nominal). Useful for validating the 'input-value plausibility' gate on K and warning that K is empirical and condition-dependent, not a fixed constant.

results.title: Allowable Stress Design Equations and Calculator | Engineers Edge
results.snippet: Confirms allowable-stress conventions and typical FoS ranges (ductile ~1.5-3 on yield, brittle higher on ultimate) used in standard design practice. Supports the safety-factor/margin verification gate and the typical-material-conventions section; cross-checks the commonly cited 1.5-4 band and the ductile-yield vs brittle-ultimate basis.

results.title: Top Design Errors in Structural Stress Analysis
results.snippet: Catalogs the most frequent stress-analysis mistakes (wrong section properties, mixing stress/pressure units, boundary condition errors, misapplied stress concentration factors). Directly supports validating the harness's 'common calculation errors / red flag' list and the materials-mechanics cheatsheet (sigma=Mc/I, section modulus).

results.title: Metrication Errors and Mishaps — NIST
results.snippet: Authoritative (NIST) catalog of real-world unit-conversion failures, including mass vs force (lbm/lbf, kg vs N) and area/volume square/cube-factor mistakes. Best-source anchor for the harness's unit/dimensional-analysis gate and the classic 'forgot to square the conversion factor' red flag.

results.title: Avoiding Singularities in FEA Boundary Conditions — Engineering.com
results.snippet: Explains stress singularities at sharp corners/point loads producing non-physical infinite stress that never converges — and that real fillet radii bound the stress. Validates red flags around stress concentration, sharp-corner modeling, and the 'order-of-magnitude / does the number make physical sense' gate.

results.title: Safety Factor: How Do I Calculate That? — FEA for All
results.snippet: Defines safety factor precisely (SF = yield load/applied or ultimate/applied) and discusses typical 2-3 margins to cover modeling error. Cross-checks the harness's safety-factor definition, margin conventions, and the distinction between yield-based and ultimate-based factors.

results.title: Civil Engineer Unit Conversion Guide — Entri
results.snippet: Practical engineering unit-conversion reference covering stress/pressure unit mixups, mass-vs-force distinction, and the always-label-units discipline. Supports the unit/dimension gate and input-value plausibility checks, though it is a blog rather than a textbook.

results.title: How to Assess Stresses with FEA — Quadco Engineering
results.snippet: Covers mesh-quality pitfalls (aspect ratio, skewness, refinement at fillets/holes), comparing FEA concentration factors against theory, and treating a blindly-trusted coarse mesh as risk. Reinforces the independent-recalculation and assumption-exposure gates plus stress-result red flags.

results.title: Bolted Joint Analysis | MechaniCalc
results.snippet: Confirms the bolt-torque cheat-sheet formula T = K·D·F (T = nut factor K x nominal diameter x preload). Critically, the variable is NOMINAL DIAMETER D, not radius — a common error to flag. States K typically 0.10-0.30 (often ~0.20 for as-received steel, lower lubricated). Verifies the proportional torque/preload model and its large uncertainty (+/-25-35%), useful for the 'red flags / assumptions exposed' gate.

results.title: K-Factor: Finding Torque Values for Bolted Joints — Hex Technology
results.snippet: Industry source detailing the nut factor (K-factor) ranges and the inherent inaccuracy of torque-based preload control. Directly supports judging the cheat-sheet's bolt formula as CORRECT in form but warns the lumped K hides friction/lubrication variability — exactly the kind of 'input validity / assumption exposure' caveat the skill should require. Good for safety-margin sanity checks on bolted joints.

results.title: Darcy friction factor formulae — Wikipedia
results.snippet: Authoritative breakdown of friction-factor selection by regime: laminar f = 64/Re (Re < ~2300, roughness-independent), Colebrook-White (implicit) and Swamee-Jain (explicit) for turbulent. Lets you verify the cheat-sheet's Darcy-Weisbach h_f = f L v^2/(2gD), the Re transition bands (2300/4000), and flag the classic error of applying turbulent correlations in the laminar regime or vice versa.

results.title: Darcy-Weisbach Equation — Nuclear Power
results.snippet: Clean statement of Darcy-Weisbach head loss and the laminar/transitional/turbulent regime boundaries (Re<2000 laminar, 2000-4000 transition, >4000 turbulent). Useful cross-check that the cheat-sheet's Reynolds definition Re = rho v D / mu and friction-factor regime mapping are stated correctly, and that f = 64/Re is only valid in laminar flow.

results.title: Basic Dynamic Load Rating — ScienceDirect Topics
results.snippet: Verifies the ISO 281 bearing-life formula L10 = (C/P)^p x 10^6 revolutions with exponent p = 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings, C = basic dynamic load rating, P = equivalent dynamic load. Confirms L10 = 90% reliability (10% failure) basis. Lets you flag the common error of using p=3 for roller bearings or confusing dynamic C with static C0.

results.title: Heat Transfer Equation Sheet (UTRGV) — Fourier, Convection, Radiation
results.snippet: University equation booklet confirming the three heat-transfer cheat-sheet formulas: conduction q = -kA dT/dx (Fourier), convection q = hA(Ts - T_inf) (Newton cooling), radiation q = epsilon*sigma*A(Ts^4 - T_inf^4) with sigma = 5.67e-8 W/m^2K^4. Key red-flag check: radiation MUST use absolute temperature (K), not Celsius — a frequent calculation error the skill should catch.

results.title: Factor of Safety — Wikipedia
results.snippet: Authoritative baseline for the skill's FoS definitions. Confirms two distinct meanings: design factor (required, chosen before design) vs. realized/safety factor (actual margin = failure stress / actual stress). Distinguishes FoS based on yield strength (ductile) vs ultimate strength (brittle), and notes that fatigue/cyclic design uses the endurance limit, not the static strength. Good for verifying the skill does not conflate 'design factor' and 'factor of safety' — a common documentation error. Also lists code-mandated ranges (e.g., aerospace ~1.5 on ultimate, structural civil higher).

results.title: Factor of Safety Explained for Engineering Design — RoyMech
results.snippet: Strong corroboration for the skill's safety-factor conventions and the Pugsley systematic-selection method (N = nsf · nm · ...). Tabulates the Pugsley factors (material quality, load control, stress-analysis accuracy, hazard to people, economic consequence) and gives typical FoS ranges by application. Useful to verify that the skill recommends a reasoned selection method rather than a single arbitrary number, and to sanity-check that quoted ranges (1.5–4 static ductile, 5–10+ for poorly-known dynamic loads) match a widely-cited engineering source.

results.title: Factor of Safety (FOS) Review — Engineers Edge
results.snippet: Reference-grade source giving the classic FoS = material strength / working stress and tabulated recommended factors by load knowledge and material (Joseph Vidosic / commonly-cited table: ~1.25–2 for well-known materials and controlled loads, up to 3–4 for average materials/static, higher for shock/uncertain loads). Good for verifying that the cheat-sheet's 'typical FoS' table values are not invented — they trace to a standard published table.

results.title: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, Ch. 6 (Fatigue) Solutions
results.snippet: Direct Shigley source for fatigue/endurance verification — the textbook the user named. Confirms the fatigue framework the skill should reference: endurance limit Se = ka·kb·kc·kd·ke·Se' (Marin factors), Se' ≈ 0.5·Sut for steels (capped ~700 MPa / 100 ksi), and Goodman/Gerber/Soderberg mean-stress criteria for finite vs infinite life. Critical for flagging the common error of using static yield strength (not Se) for cyclic loading, and for confirming fatigue FoS is defined on alternating/mean stress, not a flat multiplier.

results.title: Safety Factor — CAE Tool
results.snippet: Concise practitioner summary stating the rules the skill must get right: ductile-material safety factors are based on yield strength, cyclic-loading factors on the endurance limit, and fatigue factors differ for finite vs infinite life and ductile vs brittle. Useful as a second independent confirmation of the ductile/brittle and static/fatigue distinctions, and that brittle materials are checked against ultimate strength.

results.title: What Is Factor of Safety and How to Calculate It — TRADESAFE
results.snippet: Gives the commonly-quoted teaching ranges: ductile ~1.5–2 (small), brittle ~3–5 (larger), static ~2–4, dynamic/fatigue ~5–9. Useful as a popular-level cross-check of the cheat-sheet's headline numbers, but treat its dynamic '5–9' as illustrative rather than authoritative — note for the skill that high values often reflect uncertainty-stacking, and modern fatigue design instead uses an explicit endurance-limit calculation with a smaller FoS, so the skill should not present a flat 5–9 as the rigorous method.

results.title: Verification, Validation and Uncertainty Quantification (VVUQ) — ASME
results.snippet: Authoritative source defining the V&V vocabulary the skill should mirror: verification = does the model match the math; validation = does it match reality; plus uncertainty quantification. Directly supports judging whether the skill's verification-gate framework aligns with recognized engineering best practice and uses correct terminology (verification vs validation, not interchangeable).

results.title: An Overview of the ASME V&V-10 Guide for Verification and Validation in Computational Solid Mechanics (NCSU)
results.snippet: Open-access overview of ASME V&V-10, the recognized standard for solid-mechanics V&V. Provides the conceptual framework (code verification, solution verification, validation, sensitivity/uncertainty) against which the skill's gate system (assumption exposure, independent recalculation, margins) can be checked. Useful for grounding the V&V-process claims in a citable standard rather than ad hoc practice.

results.title: Overview of ASME V&V 20-2009 Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid Mechanics and Heat Transfer (OSTI)
results.snippet: Government-hosted overview of ASME V&V 20, covering code verification, solution verification (numerical accuracy/discretization error), and validation via experimental-uncertainty comparison. Key for validating the fluid/heat-transfer portions of the skill and for the point that validation is not a simple pass/fail but a quantified error estimate — a nuance the skill's gate design should reflect.

results.title: Sanity check — Wikipedia
results.snippet: Concise reference for the order-of-magnitude and dimensional-consistency heuristics that underpin several of the skill's proposed gates. Includes the classic worked example (power computed as 700 kJ is dimensionally wrong because joules measure energy, not power), validating the skill's units/dimensional-analysis and OOM red-flag checks as standard sanity-check practice.

results.title: Checking the Units of Engineering Calculations (A.C. Whyte)
results.snippet: Practitioner note focused specifically on dimensional/unit checking of engineering calculations — the single most reliable error-catching gate. Supports verifying that the skill's unit-and-dimensional-analysis gate and its 'common errors' list (unit mismatch, missing conversion factors) reflect established hand-calculation checking discipline.

claims.quote: a factor not derived from engineering principles but instead arrived at experimentally to make the equation valid

claims.claim: The value of K varies by roughly 300% across common applications, so torque-based preload control is highly uncertain unless verified by testing.
claims.quote: causes its value to vary about 300% across a range of common applications

claims.claim: Factor of safety (the realized/actual ratio of structural capability to applied load) is conceptually distinct from the design factor (the minimum value imposed by law, standard, or specification that a structure must meet or exceed), and the realized factor of safety must exceed the required design factor.
claims.quote: Factor of Safety (FoS): "The ratio of a structure's absolute strength (structural capability) to actual applied load; this is a measure of the reliability of a particular design." Design Factor: "A constant required value, imposed by law, standard, specification, contract or custom, to which a structure must conform or exceed." ... "The realized factor of safety must be greater than the required design factor of safety."

claims.claim: Margin of safety is defined as factor of safety minus one (MS = FoS - 1) in the common formulation, while NASA/AIAA use MS = realized factor of safety / design safety factor - 1.
claims.quote: One common definition states: "Margin of safety = factor of safety - 1" Alternative formulation used by agencies like NASA and AIAA: "Margin of safety = realized factor of safety / design safety factor - 1"

claims.claim: For ductile materials the factor of safety should be checked against both yield strength (onset of plastic deformation) and ultimate strength (failure), giving two distinct safety factors.
claims.quote: "For ductile materials, it is often required that the factor of safety be checked against both yield and ultimate strengths. The yield calculation will determine the safety factor until the part starts to deform plastically. The ultimate calculation will determine the safety factor until failure."

claims.claim: Typical factor-of-safety values vary by application: buildings ~2.0, pressure vessels ~3.5-4.0, automobiles ~3.0, aircraft/spacecraft ~1.2-4.0 (aerospace fuselage ~2.0, landing gear ~1.25).
claims.quote: Buildings: 2.0; Pressure vessels: 3.5 to 4.0; Automobiles: 3.0; Aircraft/spacecraft: 1.2 to 4.0; Aerospace fuselage: typically 2.0; landing gear: often 1.25

claims.claim: Allowable stress is defined as material strength divided by the factor of safety (allowable stress = strength / FS), the basis of the working stress / allowable stress design method.
claims.quote: "Allowable stress = material strength / factor of safety" is the fundamental concept, where allowable stress represents a material strength that has been reduced by applying a safety factor.

claims.claim: For ductile materials (e.g., steel), allowable stress is based on yield strength: sigma_a = Sy / FS.
claims.quote: For ductile materials like steel, the calculation uses yield strength: "σa = Sy / FS".

claims.claim: For brittle materials, allowable stress is based on ultimate strength: sigma_a = Su / FS.
claims.quote: For brittle materials, ultimate strength is used: "σa = Su / FS". These materials require much higher safety factors because "brittle failure is sudden and unpredictable"

claims.claim: Typical factor of safety for steel ranges from 1.5 to 2.5 depending on steel type and application, while brittle materials use much higher factors in the 6 to 10 range.
claims.quote: a factor of safety ranges from 1.5 to 2.5, depending on the type of steel and the application ... with factors "in the 6 to 10 range."

claims.claim: A design is acceptable when the actual (working) stress does not exceed the allowable stress: sigma_actual <= sigma_a.
claims.quote: A design is acceptable when "σactual ≤ σa," meaning the actual stress must not exceed the allowable stress.

claims.claim: The bolt torque-tension relationship is T = K·D·F, where T is applied torque, K is the nut factor (~0.15-0.25), D is nominal bolt diameter, and F is the desired preload force. This matches the standard short-form torque equation in Shigley and Bickford and is engineering-correct.
claims.quote: T = K × D × F ... K = Nut factor (friction coefficient), typically 0.15–0.25 ... D = Nominal bolt diameter (m) ... F = Desired preload force (N)

claims.claim: Typical nut factor values are K=0.15 for well-lubricated smooth fasteners, K=0.2 for dry steel-on-steel, and K=0.25 for rough/corroded surfaces. These values align with commonly cited handbook nut-factor tables (Bickford/Shigley) and are accurate as order-of-magnitude design values.
claims.quote: Typical values range from 0.15 for well-lubricated, precision-manufactured fasteners to 0.25 for dry, rough-surface conditions.

claims.claim: The page recommends targeting preload at 75-85% of the bolt's YIELD strength (65-75% general, 85-90% critical). This is a common but imprecise convention: standard references (Shigley) define preload as a fraction of PROOF load (Fi=0.75 Fp reusable, 0.90 Fp permanent), not yield. The percentages are in a reasonable range but the reference quantity (yield vs proof) is loosely stated and should be flagged as a 'caution' item.
claims.quote: Most applications target 75–85% of the bolt's yield strength for optimal performance. ... Critical structural applications may use 85–90%, while general-purpose applications might target 65–75%.

claims.claim: Approximately 90% of input torque is consumed by friction (split between thread friction and under-head/nut friction) and only ~10% generates useful preload. The ~10%-useful figure is a well-established Bickford rule of thumb; the specific 50% thread / 40% under-head split is plausible but the thread-vs-head allocation varies by source (often given as roughly 40% thread / 50% under-head).
claims.quote: Approximately 50% of the input torque is consumed by thread friction, 40% by friction under the bolt head or nut, and only 10% actually generates useful preload.

claims.claim: A single unit/dimension error can corrupt an entire structural stress analysis, producing wrong deflections, internal forces, and load capacity.
claims.quote: a single unit difference can disrupt the final piece of structure

claims.claim: Engineers should form preliminary assumptions/expectations (expected deflection, internal force magnitudes, size limits) before detailed analysis, e.g. by referencing similar past projects.
claims.quote: By analyzing similar projects, you can gain insights about the result.

claims.claim: FEA/CAE software produces 'error-free' and reliable results, implying computational tools eliminate calculation error.
claims.quote: Claims FEA provides "error-free calculations and reliable results"

claims.claim: A stress singularity is a point in an FEA model where a value such as stress tends to infinity, and as mesh refinement continues the stress rises without bound rather than converging — making it a key red flag distinguishing a numerical artifact from a genuine stress concentration.
claims.quote: A singularity is "a point in the model where a value, such as stress, tends to infinity." As mesh refinement continues, stresses rise unrealistically, preventing convergence and producing nonsensical results.

claims.claim: Mesh convergence is achieved when refined results vary randomly by a small amount in both directions; if results keep creeping in the same direction with refinement, that indicates a singularity rather than a genuine stress concentration. This gives a concrete verification criterion for distinguishing converged solutions from artifacts.
claims.quote: When values "vary randomly, and by a small amount, in both directions," convergence is achieved. Results "creeping in the same direction" during refinement indicate singularities rather than genuine stress concentrations.

claims.claim: Sharp internal corners produce stress singularities that do not represent physical reality, because real parts have a small fillet radius and local yielding limits the actual stress — a common modeling error to flag.
claims.quote: Stress singularities at sharp internal corners don't represent physical reality, where "there is likely to be a small radius on any internal corner." In practice, local yielding limits actual stresses in such features.

claims.claim: Point loads (force applied to a single node) create mathematically infinite stress, but per Saint-Venant's principle the local artifact is acceptable if the region is not critical and is excluded from convergence assessment, since far from the load statically equivalent loads produce essentially the same effect.
claims.quote: applying force to a single node creates infinite stress mathematically... "if the distance from the load is large enough, two different but statically equivalent loads create essentially the same effect."

claims.claim: Stress singularities also occur where fixed constraints/fixtures end, and this is especially problematic when the boundary coincides with a geometric stress concentration; remedies include elastic (spring) supports or contact modeling instead of fully fixed constraints.
claims.quote: stress singularities occur "where the fixtures end," particularly problematic when boundaries coincide with geometric stress concentrations... Elastic supports: Spring elements replace fixed constraints, eliminating singularities at boundary edges if stiffness is correctly calibrated.

claims.claim: Euler's critical buckling load for a column is F_c = π²EI/(KL)², where E is modulus of elasticity, I is the smallest area moment of inertia of the cross section, L is the unsupported length, and K is the effective length factor.
claims.quote: F_c = π²EI/(KL)² ... F_c: maximum or critical force (vertical load on column); E: modulus of elasticity; I: smallest area moment of inertia (second moment of area) of the cross section; L: unsupported length of column; K: column effective length factor, whose value depends on the conditions of end support

claims.claim: The effective length factor K depends on end conditions: K=1.0 for both ends pinned, K=0.5 for both ends fixed, K≈0.699 (~0.7) for one fixed/one pinned, and K=2.0 for one fixed/one free (cantilever).
claims.quote: Both ends pinned (hinged) | K = 1.0 ... Both ends fixed | K = 0.50 ... One fixed, one pinned | K ≈ 0.699 ... One fixed, one free (cantilever) | K = 2.0

claims.claim: The slenderness ratio is the ratio of the effective length of a column to the least radius of gyration of its cross section, and it governs whether a column fails by buckling or by direct compression.
claims.quote: the ratio of the effective length of a column to the least radius of gyration of its cross section

claims.claim: Short columns fail by direct compression (crushing/yielding) before buckling, whereas long (slender) columns fail by sudden lateral buckling in a bending mode — distinguishing the two failure regimes.
claims.quote: A short column under the action of an axial load will fail by direct compression before it buckles, but a long column loaded in the same manner will fail by springing suddenly outward laterally (buckling) in a bending mode.

claims.claim: Euler buckling theory rests on idealizing assumptions: the column is perfectly straight, made of homogeneous material, and free from initial stress.
claims.quote: an ideal column is one that is: perfectly straight, made of a homogeneous material, free from initial stress

claims.claim: The bending stress in a beam varies linearly with distance from the neutral axis and is given by sigma = -My/I (equivalently sigma = Mc/I at the extreme fiber), with M = E*kappa*I relating moment to curvature.
claims.quote: σ_xx = -M y / I (stress varies linearly with distance from neutral axis) ... M = E κ I

claims.claim: The Euler critical buckling load for a pinned-pinned column is P_cr = pi^2 * E * I / l^2, valid under assumptions of a straight beam, linear elastic material, and perfect load alignment.
claims.quote: For pinned-pinned columns, the critical buckling load: "P_cr = π²EI/l²" The analysis assumes: straight beam, linear elastic material, and perfect load alignment.

claims.claim: Torsional shear stress is tau = Tr/J, maximum at the outer surface (tau_max = T*r_o/J), and the angle of twist is theta = Tl/(GJ).
claims.quote: σ_zθ = Tr/J (maximum at outer surface: σ_max = Tr_o/J) ... θ = Tl/(GJ)

claims.quote: 3-point bending: v_max = Pl³/(48EI) ... Distributed load (simply supported): v_max = 5ql⁴/(384EI)

claims.quote: J = ∫_A r² dA ... For annular sections: J = π(r_o⁴ - r_i⁴)/2 ... Circular: J = π r⁴ / 4

claims.quote: The von Mises criterion is the standard failure prediction method for ductile materials, including structural steels, aluminium alloys and many thermoplastics.

claims.quote: These straightforward criteria apply primarily to brittle materials — those that fail by sudden fracture without appreciable plastic deformation, such as glass, ceramics, grey cast iron.

claims.quote: A common criterion is less than 5 % change in peak stress over three successive refinement levels.
